analysis.one_liner: Builds affordable housing, aids first-time buyers, protects tenants, paid for with higher estate taxes on large estates.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 21 House Democrats in August 2024, it was referred to four committees, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would put hundreds of billions of dollars into building and repairing affordable housing over a decade, pay down-payment grants for first-time buyers whose parents don't own homes, push cities to loosen zoning rules that block new housing, and give renters protections like lawyers in evictions. To pay for it, it would raise and tighten the estate tax on very large fortunes and tighten the rules wealthy families use to shield assets. It also strengthens the Community Reinvestment Act, which grades banks on how well they serve low- and moderate-income communities.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters facing eviction or displacement, low- and moderate-income families priced out of homeownership (especially first-generation buyers), public housing residents, rural and Native communities, and neighborhoods with depressed home values. Nonprofit housing developers and community lenders would receive large new funding streams.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters, first-generation homebuyers, public housing residents

how_it_helps.text: Authorizes $44.5 billion per year for the federal Housing Trust Fund and $2.5 billion per year for the Capital Magnet Fund for fiscal years 2025 through 2034, plus $70 billion for the public housing capital fund in fiscal 2025.

Creates down-payment grants of up to 3.5% of a home's value for first-time, first-generation homebuyers earning below about 120% of their area's median income, and lifts the normal income cap in high-cost areas to 140%.

Provides $2 billion per year in grants to cities and states that loosen restrictive zoning, allow denser building, and adopt tenant protections such as right-to-counsel in evictions and just-cause eviction rules.

Requires that at least 75% of homes taken back by the FHA after foreclosure be sold to owner-occupants or nonprofits that fix them up for owner-occupants, and that at least 90% of homes from covered Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac loan sales go to owner-occupants or 15-year affordable rentals.
Authorizes $5 billion in grants to states for neighborhoods where homes sell for less than the cost to build or rehabilitate them, to help underwater borrowers and fix up vacant properties.

Strengthens the Community Reinvestment Act: covers nonbank mortgage companies, deducts fossil-fuel-expansion financing from banks' community-development scores, and imposes penalties, including growth restrictions and executive pay clawbacks, on banks that fail two consecutive exams.
Overhauls the estate tax: raises rates, tightens grantor trusts and GRATs, ends certain valuation discounts and step-up in basis, and adds a surcharge on very high-income estates.

analysis.who_pays: The wealthiest households pay through higher estate taxes and closed loopholes. Large banks and nonbank mortgage companies pay through stricter CRA exams and penalties. Institutional buyers of foreclosed or delinquent mortgages face restrictions on reselling them, and landlords operating with grant funds face prevailing-wage and tenant-protection requirements.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large estates, banks, mortgage investors, landlords

drawbacks.text: The spending is enormous relative to the pay-for: the bill authorizes roughly $44.5 billion a year for the Housing Trust Fund alone for a decade, plus $70 billion for public housing and more, while estate-tax increases of the type proposed historically raise a small fraction of that; a real funding gap would add to deficits.
Down-payment grants add buyer demand in a supply-constrained market, which economists warn can push prices up rather than make homes more affordable.

Eligibility for the first-generation and first-time buyer programs rests on the borrower's self-attestation, and the bill bars creditors from liability when they rely on it in good faith, opening the door to fraudulent claims.
Expanded CRA coverage and penalties raise compliance costs for banks and nonbank mortgage companies, which could raise costs for borrowers or lead some lenders to exit low-margin markets.

The bill's estate-tax provisions would force complex re-planning by wealthy families and could complicate succession for some family-owned businesses and farms, though the text retains special valuation rules for certain farm and business real property.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real and widespread problem — housing costs — with large-scale supply investment, buyer aid, and tenant protections, and it makes the wealthy rather than general taxpayers the primary funding source. The honest objections are the scale of the spending versus the reliability of the pay-for, the risk that down-payment aid inflates prices while supply takes years to build, and self-attested eligibility that is easy to abuse. The core design is serious, not a giveaway; the funding mismatch is the biggest flaw.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to four House committees on the day it was introduced and to a subcommittee a month later, but no committee ever took it up, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Emanuel Cleaver introduced the bill on August 2, 2024, with 20 Democratic cosponsors; every initial supporter was a Democrat.
The same day, it was referred to the Financial Services, Judiciary, Veterans' Affairs, and Ways and Means Committees.
On September 13, 2024, it was referred to the Economic Opportunity Subcommittee; that was the last recorded action.
No hearing, markup, floor vote, or roll call ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Wealthy estates keep today's estate-tax rules and asset-shielding tools, and banks, nonbank mortgage companies, and bulk purchasers of delinquent loans avoid the new obligations the bill would have imposed. Renters, first-generation buyers, and public housing residents gain nothing.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on August 2, 2024 and never scheduled a markup or vote.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the bill's estate-tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill for the portion within its jurisdiction and never acted on it.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee and House Veterans' Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill for their portions of jurisdiction and never acted on it.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, none was a Republican, and the bill never reached a roll call to test broader support.

industries.note: The estate-tax title raises rates, closes GRAT, grantor-trust, and valuation-discount loopholes, and adds a surcharge on very high-income estates, exactly the families the housing spending would help are the ones who would pay for it.

The bill extends CRA examinations to nonbank mortgage originators, deducts fossil-fuel-expansion financing from community-development scores, and imposes growth restrictions and executive-pay clawbacks on repeat low performers.

Fannie, Freddie, and FHA loan sales would carry mandatory loss-mitigation duties, 90-day borrower notice, and requirements that most foreclosed homes go to owner-occupants or affordable rentals, cutting into the returns of investors who currently buy these loans cheaply.

The Housing Trust Fund, Capital Magnet Fund, Middle Class Housing Emergency Fund, and appraisal-gap grants route billions through nonprofits and state housing agencies to build and rehabilitate affordable homes.

Localities can use federal grants to adopt just-cause eviction, right-to-counsel, and anti-harassment protections, while landlords on financed projects must pay Davis-Bacon prevailing wages; owners who comply gain access to grant-funded markets.
Bank financing for fossil-fuel expansion would count against lenders' CRA scores, making some bank credit for new fossil infrastructure harder to obtain.
